deep.reconstruction:
Context: Riemann's Habilitationsschrift (1854, published 1867), §13, on functions with infinitely many maxima and minima. The previous page set up the problem. Take ∫f dx = φ(x)cos ψ(x), with φ→0 and ψ→+∞ as x→0+. Then f = φ'cos ψ − φψ' sin ψ, and ∫_0^{2π} f(x) cos n(x−a) dx splits into four integrals. The key one is J = −½∫φψ' sin(ψ+n(x−a)) dx. Its phase y = ψ(x)+n(x−a) is stationary at x=α, where ψ'(α) = −n. Since ψ' is negative and unbounded near 0, α→0 as n→∞, and ψ''(α) > 0. Write β = ψ(α)+n(α−a). Near α, y ≈ β + ψ''(α)(x−α)²/2, so dx = ±dy/√(2ψ''(α)(y−β)). The previous page obtained
−½∫_{α−ε}^{α+ε} φψ' sin y dx ≈ −[φ(α)ψ'(α)/√(2ψ''(α))] ∫_0^{ψ''(α)ε²/2} sin(y+β) dy/√y.

This page:
(1) Let ε→0 as n→∞ but so that ψ''(α)ε²/2 → ∞. Use the known Fresnel-type value ∫_0^∞ sin(y+β)/√y dy = √π sin(β+π/4). Up to lower-order terms this gives
−½∫_{α−ε}^{α+ε} φψ' sin(ψ+n(x−a)) dx ≈ −sin(β+π/4) √(π/(2ψ''(α))) φ(α)ψ'(α).
This is the stationary-phase leading term.
(2) The other parts of the Fourier integral tend to 0. So whenever this quantity does not tend to 0, the ratio of ∫_0^{2π} f(x) cos n(x−a) dx to it tends to 1.
(3) Power case. Take φ ~ x^ν (ν>0) and ψ' ~ −x^{−μ−1} (μ≥0), so ψ'' ~ x^{−μ−2}. Then φ(α)ψ'(α)/√(2ψ''(α)) is of order α^{ν−μ/2}. It does not tend to 0 when μ ≥ 2ν.
- For the earlier example φ = x^ν, ψ = 1/x: here μ = 1, α = n^{−1/2} and β = 2√n − na.
- The coefficient then grows like n^{(1−2ν)/4} for ν < 1/2. This agrees with the previous page.
(4) General criterion. Suppose xψ'(x) → ∞ in modulus, which Riemann treats as equivalent to ψ(x)/log x → ∞ as x→0.
- He uses ψ'²/ψ'' = −1/(d(1/ψ')/dx).
- Since 1/ψ' → 0, (my gloss) d(1/ψ')/dx behaves like 1/(xψ') by L'Hôpital, so it tends to 0.
- Hence φψ'/√(2ψ'') = φ/√(−2 d(1/ψ')) ~ φ/√(−2 lim 1/(xψ')).
- One can therefore choose φ→0 slowly enough that this quotient tends to ∞.
- Then ∫_x f dx = φ cos ψ has a limit as x→0, so f is improperly integrable up to 0. Yet the Fourier coefficients ∫_0^{2π} f cos n(x−a) dx do not tend to 0, and the Fourier series diverges.
(5) Interpretation. In ∫_x f dx the increments cancel because f changes sign rapidly. The factor cos n(x−a) makes them add up near the point of stationary phase.
(6) Converse statement. A function can fail to be integrable on every interval while the series Ω still converges on a dense set of x. The page begins an example using (nx) as defined earlier; the published text has the series Σ(nx)/n.
errors: No substantive errors. The asymptotic value −sin(β+π/4)√(π/(2ψ''(α)))φ(α)ψ'(α) and the order α^{ν−μ/2} are correct.

'xψ'(x) → ∞ ⇔ ψ/log x → ∞' is called 'identisch'. This holds only under regularity, e.g. monotonicity: the implication ψ/log x→∞ ⇒ xψ'→∞ can fail without it. Riemann's standing assumption of finitely many maxima and minima largely covers this.

Two things in the step φψ'/√(2ψ'') = φ/√(−2 d(1/ψ')) = φ/√(−2 lim 1/(xψ')) are loose. First, the sign is suppressed (ψ' < 0). Second, the last 'equality' is really an equality of order (L'Hôpital-type); the 'd' means the derivative d/dx.
The phrase 'für ein unendlich kleines n' (as it appears in the hand) should read 'unendlich großes n', or equivalently 'unendlich kleines α'. The published text has 'unendlich großes n'.
Interchanging the limit ε→0 with ψ''ε²→∞ and neglecting the variation of φψ' on [α−ε, α+ε] is heuristic, as is usual for stationary phase at the time.

results.what: Leading-order asymptotic of an oscillatory integral at a stationary point: ∫ g(x) sin(ψ(x)+nx) dx ≈ g(α)√(2π/ψ''(α)) sin(β+π/4), using the Fresnel integral ∫_0^∞ sin(y+β)/√y dy = √π sin(β+π/4).
results.usually_credited_to: Stokes (1856), Kelvin (1887). Riemann's 1854 use here and in his 1863 hypergeometric fragment is recognized in the literature as an early instance.

results.what: A function that is improperly (Cauchy) integrable but whose Fourier coefficients do not tend to zero, e.g. f = d/dx(x^ν cos(1/x)) with 0<ν<1/2. The general criterion is xψ'(x)→∞, i.e. ψ/log x → ∞.
results.modern_name: Failure of the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma for improper integrals; Riemann's counterexample

results.what: A trigonometric series converging on a dense set although the function is integrable on no interval (the example with (nx)).

deep.surprise_reason: This page is the manuscript of §13 of Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series. Its content, including the stationary-phase computation and the counterexample, is well known and credited to him.

checkable.asserts: φψ'/√ψ'' has order x^{ν−μ/2} for φ=x^ν and ψ' ~ x^{−μ−1} (expected 0)
For ψ=1/x the stationary point α=n^{-1/2} gives β = 2√n − na (expected 0)
α^{ν−1/2} with α=n^{-1/2} equals n^{(1−2ν)/4}, the growth rate stated on the previous page (expected 0)

transcription_corrections: 'so wird für ein unendlich kleines α[?]': the manuscript seems to read 'unendlich kleines n', a slip for 'großes n' (the published text has 'unendlich großes n').
'von gleicher Ordnung mit α^{ν−μ/2}' is confirmed.
In the general criterion, 'd' in √(−2 d(1/ψ'(x))) denotes the derivative d/dx(1/ψ'), and 'lim' applies to 1/(xψ'(x)).
The reference '(Art. 24)' at the end is doubtful: 'Art.' appears struck, and '24' may be a manuscript page reference. The published text refers to Art. 6, where (nx) is defined.
The upside-down pencil note at the bottom is unrelated and largely illegible.
